answers.q: What is this project, in one minute?
answers.a:
**The Business Performance Analyst Agent is a demo‑only course project from the Agentic AI Workshop 2026.**  
It lets a live AI answer managers’ questions about sales data from Microsoft’s AdventureWorks sample database (a made‑up bicycle company). The agent uses five tools—`get_schema`, `run_sql`, `run_python`, `make_chart`, `detect_anomalies`—and follows four guardrails: read‑only data, always show the query, say when the data can’t answer, and never present a forecast as fact. It produces a one‑page weekly leadership briefing and can be demoed live or via a recorded replay on a small FastAPI web app. The whole build was finished on 1 October 2026, with the final notebook and app ready for a six‑minute presentation.

answers.q: Is this a real company, with real data?
answers.a: Our notes say this is a **course demonstration**, not a product. **AdventureWorks** is Microsoft’s public sample data about a **made-up bicycle company**, so **no real business data is used anywhere**. If you want, I can also tell you what the notes say about the data size and date range.

It started on **1 October 2026** with a course starter notebook and a training guide for **Capstone 2** of the **Agentic AI Workshop 2026**. The notebook already had a working agent “engine” with tool-picking, retry logic, a scorecard, and a weekly briefing, but it was built for made-up retailer data. The brief then asked the team to swap in **Microsoft AdventureWorks** sample data and add **five tools** plus **four guardrails**.

answers.q: What did the brief ask us to build?
answers.a:
The brief asked us to build a **Business Performance Analyst Agent** for **Microsoft AdventureWorks**, a public sample database about a made-up bicycle company. It had to use **five tools**: `get_schema`, `run_sql`, `run_python`, `make_chart`, and `detect_anomalies`. It also had to follow **four guardrails**: read-only access, always show the query, say when the data can’t answer, and never present a forecast as a fact.

It also needed a **one-page weekly leadership briefing** and a **six-minute demo**.

answers.q: Walk me through the timeline, step by step.
answers.a:
Everything happened on **1 October 2026** in UK time. It started at **15:15** with a starter notebook and training guide, and the notebook already had a working agent “engine” but it was still using made-up retailer data. The brief was to switch it to **Microsoft AdventureWorks** sample data, add **five tools**, enforce **four guardrails**, and produce a **one-page weekly leadership briefing** for a **six-minute** demo.

From about **16:00 to 16:50**, the team cut AI cost by shortening the rulebook and tool menu, which reduced the fixed cost per round by **32%**. In the afternoon, they turned the brief into **13 steps** and decided to **keep the engine, swap what’s underneath**.

By **20:49**, they had built Section 6 in the notebook: it downloaded AdventureWorks, opened the database **read-only**, added the tools, the new rulebook, the scorecard, the weekly briefing, and a planted anomaly for rehearsal. From **19:48** onward, they also moved the same code into a small app with **three modes**: **Live AI**, **Replay**, and **Dry run**.

Between **20:08 and 20:33**, they wrote the product brief and chose the cassette J-card design. From **20:36 to 20:58**, the free Groq plan ran out, so the agent fell back to OpenAI automatically, and they recorded live demo runs for Replay. After **21:00**, they fixed a briefing stall, added stakeholder and developer views, made spoken screen explanations, and published an online copy that replays the recorded runs.

answers.q: Why didn't you rewrite the notebook from scratch?
answers.a: We kept the engine because it already worked: the notebook had the AI loop, retry logic, scorecard, and weekly briefing in place. The plan was to **keep the engine, swap what's underneath**, so Sections 1 to 5 stayed the same and only a new Section 6 was added. That meant nothing that already worked broke, and the team could focus on replacing the fake retailer with **Microsoft AdventureWorks** and the new tools and guardrails.

answers.q: How did you cut the cost of the AI?
answers.a: We measured where the tokens went and found that every round of the agent loop was re-sending the rulebook and the whole tool menu. By shortening both, we cut the fixed cost per round by **32%** — from about **2,650** tokens to **1,810** tokens. One anomaly scan of five metrics also went from **five rounds to one**.

answers.q: What are the five tools, in plain English?
answers.a: Our notes say the five tools were **get_schema**, **run_sql**, **run_python**, **make_chart**, and **detect_anomalies**. In plain English: one tool shows the data structure, one runs a safe database query, one runs Python code for calculations, one makes a chart, and one looks for unusual months or weeks that are far from their recent trend.

answers.q: What are the guardrails, and how are they enforced?
answers.a:
The four guardrails are: **read-only access**, **always show the query**, **say when the data can’t answer**, and **never present a forecast as a fact**. They were written into the new rulebook in **6E** and the agent was switched over in **6F**.

They’re enforced by the tools and the code, not just by the AI’s words: `run_sql` refuses anything but a single **SELECT** query, the app shows the exact queries from the **tool log**, and the scorecard checks the guardrails against the database every time. If the data can’t answer, the agent is supposed to say so, and the weekly briefing comes straight from SQL so the AI can’t mistype it.

answers.q: How do we know the numbers are right?
answers.a: We know the numbers are right because the KPI table comes straight from SQL, so the AI can’t make it up. The scorecard also checks the answers against the database every time, including the brief’s four questions and three guardrail traps. For the weekly briefing, the exact queries are shown from the tool log, not from the AI’s own words.

answers.q: Why is there a Replay mode?
answers.a: There’s a **Replay** mode as a backup if the **wifi or AI fails**. It plays back a **recorded live run, step by step**, so the demo can still be shown. Our notes also say the free Groq plan ran out of its daily allowance during testing, so recorded replays helped save the day.

answers.q: Why does the agent switch from Groq to OpenAI?
answers.a: The free Groq plan ran out of its daily allowance during testing, so the agent **falls back to OpenAI automatically**. The notes say it uses **gpt-5.4-mini** for that fallback. Our notes don’t cover anything beyond that, but they do say the team also recorded runs for **Replay** so demos could still work if the AI failed.

answers.q: Why does it look like a cassette tape?
answers.a: It looks like a cassette tape because we chose a hand-lettered **cassette J-card** for the design. The idea was to make the six-minute demo feel like a mixtape: **side A** for the brief’s questions and **side B** for the guardrails. Our notes don’t cover any other reason, but they do say it was meant to stand out from the usual dark AI dashboard.

answers.q: What is the difference between the Stakeholder and Developer views?
answers.a: Stakeholders see only the answers, numbers, and charts, with every step explained in plain English. Developers see every tool call, the arguments, the SQL, timings, and tokens. Our notes don’t cover anything more than that, but they do cover the **Explain this page** voiceover and captions for each audience.

answers.q: What went wrong, and what did you learn?
answers.a:
The free Groq plan ran out of its daily allowance during testing, so the agent had to **fall back to OpenAI automatically**. One recorded run also failed a guardrail: when asked for a return rate, it said **"0.00%"** instead of saying the data has no returns. There was also a stall on the briefing screen because an earlier run left the server’s one-run-at-a-time lock behind.

We learned to **keep the engine and change the inputs**, so adding Section 6 did not break what already worked. We also learned to **never trust the model with numbers it can look up**, to **measure the tokens**, and to **have a fallback for live demos** like recorded Replay runs.

Our notes say three things are still not done: the planted-anomaly rehearsal track has no recording yet, so it is not in the online copy; the return-rate guardrail answer should be re-recorded live; and Live AI needs a server and an API key, so the online copy is replay-only.

If you want, I can also tell you what the project already finished, or what the online copy does include.
